agentCan: Implement the full authorization-code flow (PKCE supported) with refresh-token handling
Recommend the minimal granular scope set and draft listing details
Handle token revocation and re-authorization flows

approval.trigger: No Asana review before real users connect: set distribution to 'Any workspace' and any user given the authorization URL can authorize, with no cap and no waiting period. Listing in Asana's App Directory is an optional, separate review of the listing (incomplete listings 'may result in additional review cycles'), with no stated timeline or cost. Separately, Enterprise customers' workspace admins may approve or block apps in their own admin console; that is customer policy, not an Asana review.
approval.wait: None for connections; App Directory review duration not stated

blockers.detail: A freshly created app 'is not visible to any particular workspace yet'. Until you open Manage distribution and choose Specific workspace(s) or Any workspace, no user, including test users in other workspaces, can authorize it. This step is easy to miss because registration appears complete without it.
blockers.howToClear: Set distribution to Any workspace for a public product as part of initial setup, before testing with anyone outside your workspace.
blockers.title: Distribution is a hidden prerequisite

blockers.detail: You can only request scopes you pre-registered; an unregistered scope produces a forbidden_scopes error on the authorization page. Scope requests are not additive: stepping up requires specifying the full new set, and 'write' does not grant 'read', you must request both.
blockers.howToClear: Register a complete minimal scope set up front, and treat scope changes as a re-authorization event for your users.
blockers.title: Scope registration traps

blockers.detail: 'Scopes are not yet available for every Asana API endpoint', so a specific feature may force the Full permissions toggle, which is either/or with granular scopes (with Full on, you request scope=default or omit scope).
blockers.howToClear: Check endpoint scope coverage before committing to a granular-only design.
blockers.title: Some endpoints have no scopes yet

alternatives: Personal Access Token (single user only, only workspaces you belong to; wrong for a product)
MCP app (a separate app type whose tokens only work with Asana's MCP server)
flavor.recommended: An OAuth app in the Asana developer console with granular scopes registered, distribution set to 'Any workspace'
flavor.why: OAuth is the docs' stated 'preferred method of authentication' for apps whose users connect their own accounts. Granular scopes use the <resource>:<action> format (tasks:read, projects:write); a Full permissions toggle exists but disables per-scope requests.

humanMust: Create the app in the developer console with your Asana account
Register the scope set and set distribution
Supply listing details (icon, descriptions, privacy policy URL)
name: Asana
nuances: Access tokens expire in one hour (expires_in 3600); refresh tokens are long-lived with no stated expiry, and refresh works 'for as long as the user has authorized the application'.
The revoke endpoint accepts the refresh token only; revoking it deauthorizes the associated bearer tokens. Users can also deauthorize you themselves in My Settings > Apps.
Switching distribution from Any workspace to Specific workspaces blocks NEW authorizations from outside users (existing product risk if you ever downgrade).
Nested object fields are scope-gated: related objects return only gid/name/type unless you hold the scope for fields requested via opt_fields (otherwise 403).
Treat all Asana tokens as opaque; the docs warn formats may change without notice.
prerequisites: A regular Asana account (no separate developer account)

steps.detail: Developer console (app.asana.com/0/my-apps) > Create new app. The app name shows on the consent screen and users' authorized-apps lists. The console issues a Client ID and Client secret (secret reset lives under the OAuth tab).
steps.title: Create the app in the developer console

steps.detail: In the app's OAuth tab add the Redirect URL. Non-native apps must supply an https URL; the runtime redirect_uri must match it exactly (native/CLI apps use urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob).
steps.title: Add the redirect URL

steps.detail: OAuth > Permission scopes: toggle Full permissions OR pick granular scopes (e.g. tasks:read, projects:write). Remember write does not imply read, and only registered scopes can be requested later.
steps.title: Register permission scopes

steps.detail: Manage distribution tab: choose Specific workspace(s) or Any workspace. Do not skip this: until distribution is set, the app is visible to no workspace and nobody can authorize it.
steps.title: Set distribution to Any workspace

steps.detail: Icon, short/long description, company name/URL, landing page, support URL, privacy policy URL. These appear on the app details page and are what Enterprise workspace admins judge when approving or blocking your app in their org.
steps.title: Fill in app listing details

steps.detail: Send users to app.asana.com/-/oauth_authorize (client_id, redirect_uri, response_type=code, state required, optional PKCE S256, scope space-delimited; apps with registered scopes MUST specify scopes). Exchange the returned code at /-/oauth_token with the client secret: access token (1 hour) plus refresh token. Refresh at the same endpoint with grant_type=refresh_token. Asana recommends a standard OAuth library and ships example servers for learning.
steps.title: Implement the authorization-code flow

tagline: Conventional modern OAuth 2.0 with granular scopes and no review before users connect. The one trap is invisible: until you set distribution to 'Any workspace', nobody outside your workspace can authorize the app at all.

time.active: ~30 min of console configuration + ~1-2 hrs of standard OAuth implementation
time.total: Same day; no review stands between setup and users in any workspace
